title: Seeing Him
hook: the believers will see their Lord as they see the moon

segments.voice: Yesterday, the garden, and your line: no eye has seen. Did something good feel like a hint of more? Today, the hope that sits at the center of that garden. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

Night. A group of companions is sitting with the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the moon is full. The companion Jarir ibn Abdullah remembers what happened next. The Prophet looked at it and spoke. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Jarir reports it: you will see your Lord as you see this moon, and you will have no trouble seeing Him. A whole crowd under one moon, and nobody pushing to get a better look. Today, seeing Him.
screen: `A FULL MOON, A CIRCLE OF FRIENDS.` → `HE LOOKS UP.` → `AS YOU SEE THIS MOON.`

segments.voice: Start with the comparison. Why the moon? Look at what the hadith itself says: you will have no trouble seeing Him. A full moon is one thing, and everyone sees it at once. Nobody has to stand in line. Nobody blocks anybody else's view. The comparison is about the seeing, clear and shared, not about Allah being like the moon. Muslim teachers are careful on that point. The Qur'an speaks of the same hope. In Pickthall's translation: "That day will faces be resplendent, Looking toward their Lord." And here the theologians from earlier in this block come back, because this was one of their real questions. Another verse says that vision does not grasp Him, while He grasps all vision. So how do the two fit together? The Ash'ari and Maturidi schools, and the Athari approach, affirm that the believers will truly see their Lord in the hereafter, and add: without asking how. The Mu'tazilah held that Allah is not seen with the eyes, and read the verses about seeing in another way. Twelver Shia theology, too, holds that He is not seen with physical eyes, and speaks of a seeing of the heart. Each side reads both verses. What they share is the hope of nearness to Allah. Why bring it in here? Because it gives the whole unseen journey of these days a direction. It isn't only escape from the fire or a stay in the garden. It's a face turned toward its Lord.
screen: `THE MOON: CLEAR, AND SEEN BY ALL.` · `FACES LOOKING TOWARD THEIR LORD.` · `THE THEOLOGIANS READ IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `A FACE TURNED TOWARD ITS LORD.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the moon. If it's night and you can see it, go and look, full or not. If it's day, or cloudy, or you're indoors, picture a full moon you remember, round and bright over a dark street. Settle, and breathe. Notice how a moon looks the same to everyone under it. Nobody owns the view. Then, slowly, let the hadith come to mind: as you see this moon. If you pray, you can hold the hope of that seeing in silence. If not, rest in the plain wonder of the light. The bell holds the time.
Seeing Him. The hope that the believers will see their Lord in the hereafter, as clearly as a crowd sees the full moon. Today's word.
Your line: like seeing the moon. Tonight, look up once, and find the moon if it's out. Tomorrow, mercy's hundred parts. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Sunni Muslims (Ash'ari, Maturidi and Athari) affirm that believers will see their Lord in the hereafter without asking how, citing this hadith and Qur'an 75:22–23; the Mu'tazilah and Twelver Shia theologians hold that Allah is not seen with physical eyes and read these texts differently.

fork.setup: you're a theologian. one verse says the faces look toward their Lord; another says vision does not grasp Him. what do you do?
options: read the two together, in your school's way.
say the question can't be asked.
fork.reveal: every school kept both verses; they differed on how the two fit, and some added: without asking how.

original.note: Arabic: seeing, vision; the theologians' word for the seeing of Allah.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hadith says God looks like the moon.
what it means: the believers' seeing of their Lord will be as clear and shared as seeing a full moon.
what a scholar hears: ru'yah, one of the classic questions of kalam, answered differently by Ash'aris, Maturidis, Atharis, Mu'tazilah and Shia.
